SSIPRD.overview: SSIPRD_ScatterInhibitBelowThisSpeed establishes the low-RPM lockout threshold below which spark scatter idle stabilization is inhibited. If an engine speed sags severely (below ~565 RPM) toward an impending stall, dithering spark timing can cause erratic combustion torque and finalize the stall. Under near-stall conditions, the ECU inhibits spark scatter dithering and focuses on solid base dwell and maximum timing recovery.
SSIPRD.overview_markdown:
`SSIPRD_ScatterInhibitBelowThisSpeed` establishes the **low-RPM lockout threshold below which spark scatter idle stabilization is inhibited**.

If an engine speed sags severely (below ~565 RPM) toward an impending stall, dithering spark timing can cause erratic combustion torque and finalize the stall. Under near-stall conditions, the ECU inhibits spark scatter dithering and focuses on solid base dwell and maximum timing recovery.
SSIPRD.tuners_guide: Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Lockout): Allows spark scatter to operate down to even lower engine speeds (e.g., 450 RPM). Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Lockout): Shuts off spark scatter at a higher speed (e.g., 750 RPM). Mopar Performance (MP) MTX Calibration Trick: As noted in the original template comments, official Mopar Performance calibrations occasionally set SSIPRD to 0xFE33 to inhibit scatter across the board and keep revs hanging slightly higher between manual gear shifts for improved drivability and rev-matching.
SSIPRD.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Lockout):**
  * Allows spark scatter to operate down to even lower engine speeds (e.g., 450 RPM).
* **Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Lockout):**
  * Shuts off spark scatter at a higher speed (e.g., 750 RPM).
* **Mopar Performance (MP) MTX Calibration Trick:**
  * As noted in the original template comments, official Mopar Performance calibrations occasionally set `SSIPRD` to `0xFE33` to inhibit scatter across the board and keep revs hanging slightly higher between manual gear shifts for improved drivability and rev-matching.
SSIPRD.operating_conditions:
`SSIPRD` is evaluated against `TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses`:
* **Evaluation:** If pulse period exceeds `SSIPRD` (meaning engine speed has dropped below ~565 RPM):
  The ECU branches to `LE312`, completely bypassing spark scatter logic.

technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
ldx  TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses ; Measured pulse period
        cpx  SSIPRD_ScatterInhibitBelowThisSpeed ; Compare to SSIPRD (0x00D0 ~ 565 RPM)
        bcc  LE312                          ; If period >= SSIPRD (RPM <= 565), inhibit scatter!

SSIPRD.calibration_notes: * **Inverse RPM Scaling:** Because pulse period is inversely proportional to engine speed, a larger word value corresponds to a lower engine speed lockout.

STFPRD.overview: STFPRD_FuelRunStartTransferPointRpm is the fuel stall-detection hysteresis threshold that drops fuel injection back from running speed-density mode into cranking enrichment mode if engine RPM sags below ~450 RPM. If an engine stalls or the driver lugs it down to near-zero speed, speed-density MAP readings become erratic and injectors cannot deliver stable fuel pulses. If engine RPM drops below STFPRD, the ECU re-engages starting/cranking fuel logic to prevent backfiring and assist the engine in catching or restarting cleanly.
STFPRD.overview_markdown:
`STFPRD_FuelRunStartTransferPointRpm` is the **fuel stall-detection hysteresis threshold** that drops fuel injection back from running speed-density mode into cranking enrichment mode if engine RPM sags below ~450 RPM.

If an engine stalls or the driver lugs it down to near-zero speed, speed-density MAP readings become erratic and injectors cannot deliver stable fuel pulses. If engine RPM drops below `STFPRD`, the ECU re-engages starting/cranking fuel logic to prevent backfiring and assist the engine in catching or restarting cleanly.
STFPRD.tuners_guide: Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Threshold): Effect: Allows the engine to drop lower in speed before re-triggering cranking fuel. Real-World Driving Feel: Prevents sudden rich bogging when lugging the engine at low speeds. Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Threshold): Effect: Re-triggers cranking fuel at a higher speed. Real-World Driving Feel: Drops back to cranking fuel sooner during stalls. If set too high, an abrupt idle dip can flood the engine with cranking fuel.
STFPRD.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Threshold):**
  * **Effect:** Allows the engine to drop lower in speed before re-triggering cranking fuel.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Prevents sudden rich bogging when lugging the engine at low speeds.
* **Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Threshold):**
  * **Effect:** Re-triggers cranking fuel at a higher speed.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Drops back to cranking fuel sooner during stalls. If set too high, an abrupt idle dip can flood the engine with cranking fuel.
STFPRD.operating_conditions:
`STFPRD` is evaluated while the engine is running:
* If `TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses` increases past `STFPRD` (engine speed drops below ~450 RPM):
  The ECU drops out of running fuel mode and returns to cranking fuel logic.

technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
LE390:  ldx  TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses
        cpx  RNFPRD_FuelStartRunTransferPointRpm ; Check Start-to-Run speed (705 RPM)
        bcs  LE3A4
        cpx  STFPRD_FuelRunStartTransferPointRpm ; Compare period to STFPRD (0x0104 ~ 450 RPM)
        bcs  LE3DA                               ; If period <= STFPRD (RPM >= 450), stay in Run Fuel
        ...                                      ; Else drop back to Cranking Fuel!

STFPRD.calibration_notes: * **Hysteresis Matching:** `RNFPRD` (~705 RPM) and `STFPRD` (~450 RPM) form the fuel hysteresis loop, mirroring the spark hysteresis loop defined by `STRNTR` (~600 RPM) and `RNSTTR` (~410 RPM).

STRNTR.overview: STRNTR_SparkStartRunTransferPointRpm defines the primary engine speed threshold required to transfer from Start Mode into Run Mode. During starter cranking, engine rotation is slow (~150-250 RPM) and irregular. The ECU remains in cranking mode, holding fixed base spark timing and dwell until the engine catches and spins up past STRNTR. Once the engine crosses above STRNTR (approximately 600 RPM) for the duration specified by SRTIME or SRTIME2, the ECU formally transitions ignition control to Run Mode.
STRNTR.overview_markdown:
`STRNTR_SparkStartRunTransferPointRpm` defines the primary **engine speed threshold required to transfer from Start Mode into Run Mode**.

During starter cranking, engine rotation is slow (~150–250 RPM) and irregular. The ECU remains in cranking mode, holding fixed base spark timing and dwell until the engine catches and spins up past `STRNTR`. Once the engine crosses above `STRNTR` (approximately 600 RPM) for the duration specified by `SRTIME` or `SRTIME2`, the ECU formally transitions ignition control to Run Mode.
STRNTR.tuners_guide: Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Threshold): What it does: Allows the engine to transfer to Run Mode at a lower RPM (e.g., 500 RPM). Real-World Driving Feel: Enables earlier engagement of dynamic spark advance and idle speed AIS stepper motor control. However, setting it too close to starter cranking speed can cause premature transfer while cranking, resulting in starter kickback or failure to catch. Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Threshold): What it does: Requires the engine to reach a higher RPM (e.g., 700-800 RPM) before entering Run Mode. Real-World Driving Feel: Ensures the engine is spinning with high momentum before transferring, but if set higher than the cold flare RPM, the engine can get "stuck" in Start Mode and fail to transition into normal running.
STRNTR.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Threshold):**
  * **What it does:** Allows the engine to transfer to Run Mode at a lower RPM (e.g., 500 RPM).
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Enables earlier engagement of dynamic spark advance and idle speed AIS stepper motor control. However, setting it too close to starter cranking speed can cause premature transfer while cranking, resulting in starter kickback or failure to catch.
* **Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Threshold):**
  * **What it does:** Requires the engine to reach a higher RPM (e.g., 700–800 RPM) before entering Run Mode.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Ensures the engine is spinning with high momentum before transferring, but if set higher than the cold flare RPM, the engine can get "stuck" in Start Mode and fail to transition into normal running.
STRNTR.operating_conditions:
`STRNTR` is evaluated during every distributor pulse while the ECU is in Start Mode:
* **Measured Variable:** `TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses` (16-bit pulse period).
* **Evaluation:** If `STRNTR - TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses >= 0` (meaning pulse period is less than or equal to `STRNTR`, or RPM $\ge$ ~600 RPM), the ECU branches to increment the consecutive start-to-run pulse counter (`Timer_NormalDwell`).

technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
ldd  STRNTR_SparkStartRunTransferPointRpm ; Load 16-bit threshold (0x00C3 ~ 600 RPM)
        subd TimerOverflowsBetweenDistPulses      ; Compare against measured period
        bcc  ENGINE_IDLING_BETWEEN598_813RPM      ; If period <= STRNTR (RPM >= 600), branch!
        ...

STRNTR.calibration_notes: * **Hysteresis Pair:** `STRNTR` works as a hysteresis pair with `RNSTTR` (~410 RPM). Once in Run Mode, the engine must drop below `RNSTTR` before it will drop back into Start Mode.

During starter cranking, engine rotation is slow (~150-250 RPM) and irregular. The ECU remains in cranking mode, holding fixed base spark timing and dwell until the engine catches and spins up past STRNTR. Once the engine crosses above STRNTR (approximately 600 RPM) for the duration specified by SRTIME or SRTIME2, the ECU formally transitions ignition control to Run Mode. | TUNER'S GUIDE: Increasing the Value (Lower RPM Threshold): What it does: Allows the engine to transfer to Run Mode at a lower RPM (e.g., 500 RPM). Real-World Driving Feel: Enables earlier engagement of dynamic spark advance and idle speed AIS stepper motor control. However, setting it too close to starter cranking speed can cause premature transfer while cranking, resulting in starter kickback or failure to catch. Decreasing the Value (Higher RPM Threshold): What it does: Requires the engine to reach a higher RPM (e.g., 700-800 RPM) before entering Run Mode. Real-World Driving Feel: Ensures the engine is spinning with high momentum before transferring, but if set higher than the cold flare RPM, the engine can get "stuck" in Start Mode and fail to transition into normal running.

THRKNK.overview: THRKNK_DeltaAbove_MINTHR defines the throttle opening threshold above base idle position required to trigger the low-RPM knock retard limit (KNKLIM). The ECU tracks the minimum historical TPS voltage recorded during the driving session (MINTHR_LowestSessionTPS). When the throttle is opened beyond MINTHR by more than THRKNK while operating below KLMRPM, the ECU activates the low-RPM knock protection ceiling.
THRKNK.overview_markdown:
`THRKNK_DeltaAbove_MINTHR` defines the **throttle opening threshold above base idle position** required to trigger the low-RPM knock retard limit (`KNKLIM`).

The ECU tracks the minimum historical TPS voltage recorded during the driving session (`MINTHR_LowestSessionTPS`). When the throttle is opened beyond `MINTHR` by more than `THRKNK` while operating below `KLMRPM`, the ECU activates the low-RPM knock protection ceiling.
THRKNK.tuners_guide: Increasing the Value (Higher Throttle Delta): Requires a larger throttle opening before the low-RPM KNKLIM clamp activates, allowing the standard RETMAX curve to operate over a broader throttle range. Decreasing the Value (Lower Throttle Delta): Engages the low-RPM KNKLIM retard clamp on lighter pedal movements. Stock Setting: 0x53 equals (83 / 255) 5.0V ~ 1.63 Volts above minimum idle TPS.
THRKNK.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Increasing the Value (Higher Throttle Delta):**
  * Requires a larger throttle opening before the low-RPM `KNKLIM` clamp activates, allowing the standard `RETMAX` curve to operate over a broader throttle range.
* **Decreasing the Value (Lower Throttle Delta):**
  * Engages the low-RPM `KNKLIM` retard clamp on lighter pedal movements.
* **Stock Setting:**
  * `0x53` equals $\frac{83}{255} \times 5.0\text{V} \approx 1.63\text{ Volts}$ above minimum idle TPS.
THRKNK.operating_conditions:
`THRKNK` is evaluated inside `KnockDetect_MM`:
* **Evaluation:** Delta TPS ($\text{TpsVolts} - \text{MINTHR}$) is compared against `THRKNK`.
* **Action:** If Delta TPS $\ge$ `THRKNK` and RPM < `KLMRPM`, the ECU overrides the normal MAP knock retard curve with the constant `KNKLIM`.

technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
ldab TpsVolts
        subb MINTHR_LowestSessionTPS ; Delta TPS above base idle
        bcs  LD489
        cmpb THRKNK_DeltaAbove_MINTHR ; Compare against THRKNK (0x53)
        bcs  LD489                   ; If below THRKNK, use RETMAX
        ldab EngineRpm_HB
        cmpb KLMRPM_MinKnockDetectRpm ; Check RPM
        bcc  LD489
        ldaa KNKLIM_MaxKnockRetard    ; Apply low-RPM clamp
        bra  LD48C

THRKNK.calibration_notes: * **Adaptive Baseline:** Because `MINTHR` dynamically learns the lowest TPS voltage on every key cycle, `THRKNK` represents a true relative delta regardless of mechanical throttle cable slack or TPS sensor installation angle.

TMPSWP.overview: TMPSWP_EngTempSwitchPointForSparkAdvance is the primary coolant temperature threshold that divides the ECU's ignition timing logic into two distinct modes: Cold Engine Operation and Warm (Normal) Engine Operation. Cold engines have lower combustion chamber temperatures, slower fuel vaporization, and slower flame propagation speeds, requiring a dedicated ignition advance strategy (CLDMAP) to maintain stability and warm up the engine quickly. Once the coolant reaches normal operating temperature, the ECU switches to its primary warm timing tables (HOTMAP and WOTMAP). TMPSWP defines the exact temperature where this transition occurs.
TMPSWP.overview_markdown:
`TMPSWP_EngTempSwitchPointForSparkAdvance` is the primary coolant temperature threshold that divides the ECU's ignition timing logic into two distinct modes: **Cold Engine Operation** and **Warm (Normal) Engine Operation**.

Cold engines have lower combustion chamber temperatures, slower fuel vaporization, and slower flame propagation speeds, requiring a dedicated ignition advance strategy (`CLDMAP`) to maintain stability and warm up the engine quickly. Once the coolant reaches normal operating temperature, the ECU switches to its primary warm timing tables (`HOTMAP` and `WOTMAP`). `TMPSWP` defines the exact temperature where this transition occurs.
TMPSWP.tuners_guide: Increasing the Value (Higher Temp Threshold): What it does: Forces the engine to stay in cold-engine ignition mode longer into its warmup cycle. Effect on Total Timing: Extends the use of CLDMAP. Total timing will follow cold advance tables until the engine reaches a higher coolant temperature. Real-World Driving Feel: Useful if an engine exhibits cold-stumble or hesitation during extended warm-ups, but setting it too high causes sluggish throttle response and poor fuel economy once the vehicle is being driven. Decreasing the Value (Lower Temp Threshold): What it does: Causes the ECU to switch into warm-engine spark logic earlier during warm-up. Effect on Total Timing: Engages HOTMAP and WOTMAP sooner after startup. Real-World Driving Feel: Can improve throttle response earlier during warm-up, but if set too low (e.g., below the thermostat opening temperature), a cold engine may encounter poor drivability or detonation under load due to insufficient warmup timing. Typical Tuning Practice: In stock calibrations, TMPSWP is set to 0xA6 (~166 degF / 74 degC), matching the factory 180 degF thermostat warm-up curve. If running a cooler thermostat (such as a 160 degF unit), tuners occasionally lower this constant slightly so the ECU consistently enters warm-engine spark mode.
TMPSWP.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Increasing the Value (Higher Temp Threshold):**
  * **What it does:** Forces the engine to stay in cold-engine ignition mode longer into its warmup cycle.
  * **Effect on Total Timing:** Extends the use of `CLDMAP`. Total timing will follow cold advance tables until the engine reaches a higher coolant temperature.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Useful if an engine exhibits cold-stumble or hesitation during extended warm-ups, but setting it too high causes sluggish throttle response and poor fuel economy once the vehicle is being driven.

* **Decreasing the Value (Lower Temp Threshold):**
  * **What it does:** Causes the ECU to switch into warm-engine spark logic earlier during warm-up.
  * **Effect on Total Timing:** Engages `HOTMAP` and `WOTMAP` sooner after startup.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Can improve throttle response earlier during warm-up, but if set too low (e.g., below the thermostat opening temperature), a cold engine may encounter poor drivability or detonation under load due to insufficient warmup timing.

* **Typical Tuning Practice:**
  * In stock calibrations, `TMPSWP` is set to `0xA6` (~166°F / 74°C), matching the factory 180°F thermostat warm-up curve. If running a cooler thermostat (such as a 160°F unit), tuners occasionally lower this constant slightly so the ECU consistently enters warm-engine spark mode.
TMPSWP.operating_conditions:
`TMPSWP` is evaluated on every execution pass of the main spark advance routine (`CalculateSparkAdvance_MM`):

* **Evaluated Input:** `CoolantTemp` (analog-to-digital reading of the Coolant Temperature Sensor, stored in RAM).
* **Cold Path (`CoolantTemp < TMPSWP`):** The ECU branches to the cold MAP advance table (`CLDMAP`) and applies cold closed-throttle clamping (`CLDLMT`).
* **Warm Path (`CoolantTemp >= TMPSWP`):** The ECU branches to warm spark advance logic, selecting between part-throttle (`HOTMAP`) and full-throttle (`WOTMAP`).

technical_mechanics.text:
Inside `T-LMv13.asm` at line 6561:



### Logic Summary:
$$\text{Branch Condition} = \begin{cases} \text{Warm Spark Path (LEFD2)}, & \text{if } \text{CoolantTemp} \ge \text{TMPSWP} \\ \text{Cold Spark Path (CLDMAP)}, & \text{if } \text{CoolantTemp} < \text{TMPSWP} \end{cases}$$
technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
CalculateSparkAdvance_MM:
           clrb                ; b = 0
           clra                ; a = 0
           std  Temp0          ; Clear Temp0 and Temp1 in RAM
           ldaa MapValue       ; Load A with current MAP sensor reading
           ldab CoolantTemp    ; Load B with current coolant temperature
           cmpb TMPSWP_EngTempSwitchPointForSparkAdvance ; Compare CoolantTemp to TMPSWP (0xA6)
           bcc  LEFD2          ; If CoolantTemp >= TMPSWP, branch to Warm Spark Logic (LEFD2)

           ; --- COLD ENGINE SPARK PATH ---
           ldx  #CLDMAP_AdvanceFromMAPCold
           jsr  Lookup4ByteTable
           ...

TMPSWP.calibration_notes:
* **Coupled Fuel Switch:** Note that the fuel system also has its own temperature thresholds for closed-loop O2 operation and enrichment. Adjusting `TMPSWP` alters ignition timing transitions independently of fuel transitions.
* **Hysteresis:** There is no hysteresis band on `TMPSWP` itself; it is a single-byte unsigned comparison. Once coolant crosses this threshold, the warm spark path is taken immediately.

WOTMAP.overview: WOTMAP_AdvanceFromMAPWarmFull is the primary full-throttle / wide-open throttle (WOT) load advance table. It establishes the base ignition advance curve as a function of intake manifold pressure whenever the engine is operated at wide-open throttle under warm conditions. At WOT, volumetric efficiency is maximized, cylinder pressures are at their peak, and combustion chamber temperatures rise rapidly-especially under turbocharger boost. Because high charge density drastically accelerates flame front speeds, ignition timing must be retarded under boost to keep peak cylinder pressure (PCP) safely timed after top dead center (typically ~14-17 deg ATDC) and prevent destructive detonation. In addition to serving as the WOT ignition curve, WOTMAP serves as the absolute minimum advance floor for warm part-throttle boost timing via the HOTMAP blending logic.
WOTMAP.overview_markdown:
`WOTMAP_AdvanceFromMAPWarmFull` is the primary full-throttle / wide-open throttle (WOT) load advance table. It establishes the base ignition advance curve as a function of intake manifold pressure whenever the engine is operated at wide-open throttle under warm conditions.

At WOT, volumetric efficiency is maximized, cylinder pressures are at their peak, and combustion chamber temperatures rise rapidly—especially under turbocharger boost. Because high charge density drastically accelerates flame front speeds, ignition timing must be retarded under boost to keep peak cylinder pressure (PCP) safely timed after top dead center (typically ~14–17° ATDC) and prevent destructive detonation.

In addition to serving as the WOT ignition curve, `WOTMAP` serves as the **absolute minimum advance floor** for warm part-throttle boost timing via the `HOTMAP` blending logic.
WOTMAP.tuners_guide: Total full-throttle ignition timing is calculated as the base RPM advance (GOVNER) plus the MAP advance from WOTMAP: Total WOT Advance ~ GOVNER(RPM) + WOTMAP(MAP) - AntiLagRetard - KnockRetard +/- BaroTrims Increasing Table Values (Adding Timing in WOTMAP): Effect on Total Timing: Advances full-throttle ignition timing across the corresponding boost/MAP points. Real-World Driving Feel: Increases peak torque, accelerates spool-up, and improves high-RPM horsepower. Cautions: Extremely critical for engine safety! Excessive advance under boost rapidly causes heavy detonation, blown head gaskets, or melted ring lands. Always tune with a knock monitor and appropriate fuel octane. Decreasing Table Values (Pulling Timing in WOTMAP): Effect on Total Timing: Retards full-throttle ignition timing under boost. Real-World Driving Feel: Produces a safe, knock-resistant tune (ideal for low-octane fuel or high boost), but excessive retard causes sluggish power delivery and very high exhaust gas temperatures (EGTs), which can overheat turbochargers and exhaust valves.
WOTMAP.tuners_guide_markdown:
Total full-throttle ignition timing is calculated as the base RPM advance (`GOVNER`) plus the MAP advance from `WOTMAP`:

$$\text{Total WOT Advance} \approx \text{GOVNER}(\text{RPM}) + \text{WOTMAP}(\text{MAP}) - \text{AntiLagRetard} - \text{KnockRetard} \pm \text{BaroTrims}$$

* **Increasing Table Values (Adding Timing in `WOTMAP`):**
  * **Effect on Total Timing:** Advances full-throttle ignition timing across the corresponding boost/MAP points.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Increases peak torque, accelerates spool-up, and improves high-RPM horsepower.
  * **Cautions:** Extremely critical for engine safety! Excessive advance under boost rapidly causes heavy detonation, blown head gaskets, or melted ring lands. Always tune with a knock monitor and appropriate fuel octane.
* **Decreasing Table Values (Pulling Timing in `WOTMAP`):**
  * **Effect on Total Timing:** Retards full-throttle ignition timing under boost.
  * **Real-World Driving Feel:** Produces a safe, knock-resistant tune (ideal for low-octane fuel or high boost), but excessive retard causes sluggish power delivery and very high exhaust gas temperatures (EGTs), which can overheat turbochargers and exhaust valves.
WOTMAP.operating_conditions:
`WOTMAP` is engaged under the following conditions:
1. **Engine is Warm:** Coolant temperature is at or above `TMPSWP` ($\ge 166^\circ\text{F} / 74^\circ\text{C}$).
2. **Throttle is Wide-Open (WOT):** Bit 0 of `BitFlags_81` is `1` (Full Throttle flag set).
   - In this mode, the part-throttle blending calculation (`HOTMAP` and `ARADVR`) is completely bypassed.
3. **Part-Throttle Floor:** During part throttle under boost, if `HOTMAP` minus the `ARADVR` retard drops below `WOTMAP`, the ECU clamps timing to `WOTMAP`.

technical_mechanics.text:
Inside `T-LMv13.asm` (lines 6587–6599):



### Table Data (Stock A171 Calibration):
```
Number of points: 4
Point 1: MAP = 0x66 (14 inHg vac) -> Advance = 0x14 (+20 / 2 = +10.0°)
Point 2: MAP = 0x70 (11 inHg vac) -> Advance = 0x00 (0 / 2   = +0.0°)
Point 3: MAP = 0x92 (1.4 psi boost) -> Advance = 0xEE (-18 / 2 = -9.0°)
Point 4: MAP = 0xB6 (7.1 psi boost) -> Advance = 0xE6 (-26 / 2 = -13.0°)
```
*(Advance values are signed 8-bit integers where 1 bit = 0.5° crankshaft advance).*
technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
LEFD2:  ldab BitFlags_81    ; Check throttle state
        bpl  LEFB5          ; Branch if closed throttle / idle
        ldx  #WOTMAP_AdvanceFromMAPWarmFull
        jsr  Lookup4ByteTable ; A = WOTMAP(MapValue)

        ; Subtract anti-lag timing if active
        suba AntiLagRetard
        staa Temp0          ; Store WOTMAP timing into Temp0

        ldab BitFlags_81    ; Check WOT flag
        lsrb                ; Shift bit 0 (Full Throttle) into Carry
        bcs  LF027          ; If WOT, jump directly to Baro comp (bypasses HOTMAP!)
        ...

WOTMAP.calibration_notes:
* **MPTune 3D Display (`FTTIME`):**  
  In MPTune, `FullThrottleTiming` (`FTTIME`) is a **calculated display table** created by adding `GOVNER` and `WOTMAP`. It does not exist as an independent 3D lookup table in the ECU firmware.
* **Anti-Lag Retard (`ANTLAG`):** Notice line 6593: `suba AntiLagRetard`. In Turbonator-LM calibrations, launch anti-lag retard is subtracted specifically from `Temp0` immediately after the `WOTMAP` lookup.

PTPWOF.overview: PTPWOF is the boost-onset fuel rate adder for part-throttle driving. Think of it as a progressive power-valve spring and jet combo built into the computer's fuel injection logic. When you are cruising at light throttle, your engine runs on normal manifold vacuum, and the ECU delivers fuel strictly according to your base cruise fuel map (MAPTBL_FuelPartThrottle). But on a turbocharged engine, if you roll into the gas pedal to pass a car or pull up a grade on the highway, the turbo spools up and boosts the intake manifold-even though your foot has not mashed the gas pedal to the floor. As manifold pressure climbs past roughly 5 pounds of boost, air density shoots up rapidly. If the computer only looked at the vacuum cruise fuel map, the mixture would instantly go lean and cause dangerous detonation (spark knock) or a flat-spot stumble. PTPWOF solves this by calculating how far your boost pressure is above that ~5 psi threshold and immediately multiplying that extra pressure by this calibration setting. It adds that extra squirt of fuel directly on top of your normal cruise pulse width, keeping air/fuel ratios safely rich while the turbo builds boost, all without washing down the cylinders during normal light-load vacuum cruise.
PTPWOF.overview_markdown:
`PTPWOF` is the **boost-onset fuel rate adder** for part-throttle driving. Think of it as a progressive power-valve spring and jet combo built into the computer's fuel injection logic.

When you are cruising at light throttle, your engine runs on normal manifold vacuum, and the ECU delivers fuel strictly according to your base cruise fuel map (`MAPTBL_FuelPartThrottle`). But on a turbocharged engine, if you roll into the gas pedal to pass a car or pull up a grade on the highway, the turbo spools up and boosts the intake manifold—even though your foot has not mashed the gas pedal to the floor.

As manifold pressure climbs past roughly 5 pounds of boost, air density shoots up rapidly. If the computer only looked at the vacuum cruise fuel map, the mixture would instantly go lean and cause dangerous detonation (spark knock) or a flat-spot stumble. 

`PTPWOF` solves this by calculating how far your boost pressure is above that ~5 psi threshold and immediately multiplying that extra pressure by this calibration setting. It adds that extra squirt of fuel directly on top of your normal cruise pulse width, keeping air/fuel ratios safely rich while the turbo builds boost, all without washing down the cylinders during normal light-load vacuum cruise.
PTPWOF.tuners_guide: Physical Effects of Raising vs. Lowering: Raising the Value (Richer Boost Spool): Delivers more extra fuel for every pound of boost you make under part-throttle acceleration. If your engine feels like it hesitates, surges, or pings as boost begins building at half-throttle, bumping this value up will richen the mixture and smooth out turbo spool-up. Lowering the Value (Leaner Boost Spool): Decreases the extra fuel added per pound of boost. If the car stumbles, puffs black smoke, or feels sluggish and boggy when rolling into boost at partial throttle, lowering this value will clean up the transition. Edge Cases: Setting to Zero: Completely disables the part-throttle boost adder. The engine will receive zero supplemental fuel as boost builds until either wide-open throttle is hit or the computer maxes out the base cruise table. This will cause a severe lean condition, backfiring through the intake, or piston-damaging detonation under part-throttle boost! Setting to Maximum: Forces the boost-added pulse width to jump straight to the full-throttle ceiling (WOTTBL) the moment you cross the boost threshold (~5 psi). While fuel delivery will not exceed what the engine gets at wide-open throttle due to the safety clamp, having full WOT fueling at mere partial throttle will make the engine run excessively rich, causing sluggish spool-up, soggy acceleration, and black exhaust smoke. Real-World Tuning Scenarios: Why Upgrading to a 3-Bar MAP Sensor Requires RAISING This Setting: A 2-bar MAP sensor reads from full vacuum up to ~14.7 psi of boost across its full voltage range. A 3-bar sensor squeezes double the boost range (up to ~29.4 psi) across that same voltage range. Because each unit of voltage on a 3-bar sensor represents 50% more pressure, the computer sees fewer counts per pound of boost (it counts 1.5 times slower). If you left this setting alone after swapping to a 3-bar sensor, the computer would only add about 67% of the extra fuel it used to add for every pound of boost, causing the engine to lean out during part-throttle spool-up! Rule of thumb for 3-bar conversion: Multiply this setting by 1.5 (a 50% increase) to restore the factory fuel adder rate per pound of boost. (You will also lower OBCONST from 170 down to 113 to keep the boost trigger at ~5 psi). Why Upgrading to Larger Injectors (+20%, +40%, etc.) Requires LOWERING This Setting: Larger injectors flow more fuel for every millisecond the nozzle is pulsed open. If you install +40% injectors (which flow ~1.4 times as much fuel), leaving this pulse width adder alone will squirt 40% too much fuel into the engine, causing it to bog and puff black smoke when the turbo spools at partial throttle. Rule of thumb for injector changes: Divide this setting by your injector flow multiplier (e.g., divide by 1.20 for +20% injectors, or divide by 1.40 for +40% injectors). The Combined Real-World Math (3-Bar MAP + Bigger Injectors): Notice that upgrading to a 3-bar MAP pulls this setting UP (x 1.5), while bigger injectors pull this setting DOWN (/ 1.4). When you do both at the same time, the two changes partially cancel each other out: New Setting = Base Setting * 1.5 (for 3-bar) / Injector Multiplier For example, moving from a stock 2-bar setup with stock injectors (stock setting ~7,858) to a 3-bar setup with +20% to +40% injectors results in a net setting of ~9,451 (an overall increase of ~20%), exactly as configured in Stage IV calibrations! Bigger Turbochargers & Aggressive Cams: Large aftermarket turbos often build boost later and hit harder. If your wideband O2 gauge shows a brief lean spike right as the turbo hits 5-10 psi under medium pedal travel, nudge this value up 5% to 10% to provide the necessary fuel cushion to keep combustion stable and exhaust gas temperatures safe.
PTPWOF.tuners_guide_markdown:
- **Physical Effects of Raising vs. Lowering:**
  - **Raising the Value (Richer Boost Spool):** Delivers more extra fuel for every pound of boost you make under part-throttle acceleration. If your engine feels like it hesitates, surges, or pings as boost begins building at half-throttle, bumping this value up will richen the mixture and smooth out turbo spool-up.
  - **Lowering the Value (Leaner Boost Spool):** Decreases the extra fuel added per pound of boost. If the car stumbles, puffs black smoke, or feels sluggish and boggy when rolling into boost at partial throttle, lowering this value will clean up the transition.
- **Edge Cases:**
  - **Setting to Zero:** Completely disables the part-throttle boost adder. The engine will receive zero supplemental fuel as boost builds until either wide-open throttle is hit or the computer maxes out the base cruise table. This will cause a severe lean condition, backfiring through the intake, or piston-damaging detonation under part-throttle boost!
  - **Setting to Maximum:** Forces the boost-added pulse width to jump straight to the full-throttle ceiling (`WOTTBL`) the moment you cross the boost threshold (~5 psi). While fuel delivery will not exceed what the engine gets at wide-open throttle due to the safety clamp, having full WOT fueling at mere partial throttle will make the engine run excessively rich, causing sluggish spool-up, soggy acceleration, and black exhaust smoke.
- **Real-World Tuning Scenarios:**
  - **Why Upgrading to a 3-Bar MAP Sensor Requires RAISING This Setting:**
    - A 2-bar MAP sensor reads from full vacuum up to ~14.7 psi of boost across its full voltage range. A 3-bar sensor squeezes double the boost range (up to ~29.4 psi) across that same voltage range.
    - Because each unit of voltage on a 3-bar sensor represents 50% more pressure, the computer sees fewer counts per pound of boost (it counts 1.5 times slower).
    - If you left this setting alone after swapping to a 3-bar sensor, the computer would only add about 67% of the extra fuel it used to add for every pound of boost, causing the engine to lean out during part-throttle spool-up!
    - **Rule of thumb for 3-bar conversion:** Multiply this setting by **1.5** (a 50% increase) to restore the factory fuel adder rate per pound of boost. (You will also lower `OBCONST` from 170 down to 113 to keep the boost trigger at ~5 psi).
  - **Why Upgrading to Larger Injectors (+20%, +40%, etc.) Requires LOWERING This Setting:**
    - Larger injectors flow more fuel for every millisecond the nozzle is pulsed open.
    - If you install +40% injectors (which flow ~1.4 times as much fuel), leaving this pulse width adder alone will squirt 40% too much fuel into the engine, causing it to bog and puff black smoke when the turbo spools at partial throttle.
    - **Rule of thumb for injector changes:** Divide this setting by your injector flow multiplier (e.g., divide by 1.20 for +20% injectors, or divide by 1.40 for +40% injectors).
  - **The Combined Real-World Math (3-Bar MAP + Bigger Injectors):**
    - Notice that upgrading to a 3-bar MAP pulls this setting **UP** (x 1.5), while bigger injectors pull this setting **DOWN** (/ 1.4).
    - When you do both at the same time, the two changes partially cancel each other out:
      `New Setting = Base Setting * 1.5 (for 3-bar) / Injector Multiplier`
    - For example, moving from a stock 2-bar setup with stock injectors (stock setting ~7,858) to a 3-bar setup with +20% to +40% injectors results in a net setting of ~9,451 (an overall increase of ~20%), exactly as configured in Stage IV calibrations!
  - **Bigger Turbochargers & Aggressive Cams:** Large aftermarket turbos often build boost later and hit harder. If your wideband O2 gauge shows a brief lean spike right as the turbo hits 5–10 psi under medium pedal travel, nudge this value up 5% to 10% to provide the necessary fuel cushion to keep combustion stable and exhaust gas temperatures safe.
PTPWOF.operating_conditions:
This boost fuel adder kicks in only when specific real-world engine conditions are met:

1. **Part Throttle (Cruising & Passing):**
   - The throttle must be cracked open off idle, but **not** floored to wide-open throttle (WOT).
   - Once you floor the gas pedal to 100% wide-open throttle, the computer immediately switches over to the dedicated full-throttle power fuel curve (`WOTTBL_FuelFullThrottle`), completely bypassing this part-throttle calculation.
2. **Positive Boost / High Engine Load:**
   - Boost must rise above the boost transition threshold (roughly 4.9 to 5.0 psi of boost, set by `OBCONST_OverboostConstant1`).
   - In deep vacuum (idle, steady downhill cruise, light city driving), this boost adder stays completely dormant and adds zero fuel.
3. **Timed Acceleration Enrichment:**
   - If you sustain aggressive acceleration long enough or rev high enough under load, the ECU automatically transitions to full open-loop power enrichment.

technical_mechanics.text:
Inside `T-LMv13.asm` (lines 4306–4330):



### Register Trace & Mathematical Formulas:
1. **Load & Test MAP against `OBCONST`:**
   - Register `A` is loaded with `MapValue`. Register `B` holds `Timer_OpenLoopFraction`.
   - `cmpa OBCONST_OverboostConstant1`: Tests if manifold pressure has crossed the boost threshold.
   - If `MapValue >= OBCONST`: `tba` copies `Timer_OpenLoopFraction` into `A` and branches to `LDF43`.
   - If `MapValue < OBCONST`: `aba` adds `Timer_OpenLoopFraction` to `MapValue`. If carry is set, accumulator `A` saturates at `0xFF`. Then `suba OBCONST_OverboostConstant1` subtracts the boost threshold. If the result is less than or equal to zero (`bls LDF50`), no offset is added (`Temp7` remains `0x0000`).
2. **16-Bit Fixed-Point Multiplication (`mul16bit`):**
   - At `LDF43`, accumulator `A` contains the effective delta load factor, which is saved to RAM variable `Temp5`.
   - Register `D` is loaded with the 16-bit word `PTPWOF_PartThrottlePulsewidthOffset` (`0x24EB`).
   - The subroutine `mul16bit` computes:
     `Result D = (Temp5 * PTPWOF) / 256`
   - The resulting 16-bit pulsewidth offset is stored in RAM variable `Temp7`.
3. **Table Blending & Baseline Limiting:**
   - The base part-throttle pulsewidth is looked up from `MAPTBL_FuelPartThrottle` using `Lookup5ByteTable` and added to `Temp7`:
     `Combined PW = MAPTBL(MapValue) + Temp7`
   - The ECU then compares this sum against `FuelBaselineResult` (the full-throttle value previously looked up from `WOTTBL_FuelFullThrottle`):
     `subd FuelBaselineResult`
   - If `Combined PW < FuelBaselineResult` (`bcs LDF64`), the blended part-throttle pulsewidth is kept; otherwise, it is clamped to `FuelBaselineResult` at `LDF62`.
technical_mechanics.assembly_code:
LDF2F:  ldaa MapValue       ; load a with memory contents
           cmpa OBCONST_OverboostConstant1    ; compare a with memory contents (data is aa)
           bcs  LDF39          ; branch if lower
           tba                 ; a = b
           bra  LDF43          ; branch

   LDF39:  aba                 ; a=a+b
           bcc  LDF3E          ; branch if greater or equal
           ldaa #0xff          ; load a with value -11111111-
   LDF3E:  suba OBCONST_OverboostConstant1    ;  (data is aa)
           bls  LDF50          ; branch if lower or same
   LDF43:  clrb                ; b = 0
           stab Counter_PrimaryAndSecondaryRamp    ; store b into memory
           staa Temp5          ; store a into memory
           ldd  PTPWOF_PartThrottlePulsewidthOffset    ;  (data is 1eb2)
           jsr  mul16bit
           std  Temp7          ; store D to RAM
   LDF50:  ldaa MapValue       ; load a with memory contents
           ldx  #MAPTBL_FuelPartThrottle    ; load index with value
   LDF55:  jsr  Lookup5ByteTable
           addd Temp7          ; d = d + memory contents
           std  Temp7          ; store D to RAM
           subd FuelBaselineResult    ; d = d - memory contents
           ldd  Temp7          ; load d (a&b) with memory contents
           bcs  LDF64          ; branch if lower

PTPWOF.calibration_notes:
- **Codebase Origins & Naming:**
  In the baseline A171 disassembly, this constant was labeled `FPWUNK` (*FuelPulsewidthFunctionUnknown*). In the Turbonator Stage IV code for this calibration, Rob Lloyd relabeled it `PTPWOF` (*PartThrottlePulsewidthOffset*). Both share the exact same `.org 0xc1e2` location in ROM.
- **Tied Directly to the Boost Fuel Threshold:**
  This parameter is completely inactive during normal vacuum cruise. It only starts spraying extra fuel once intake manifold boost passes the boost fuel threshold (set by `OBCONST_OverboostConstant1`, typically around 5 pounds of boost).
- **Built-in Safety Ceiling:**
  The computer has a built-in safety clamp: no matter how high you set this part-throttle fuel adder, the total fuel delivered at partial throttle will never exceed what the engine would get at full wide-open throttle (`WOTTBL_FuelFullThrottle`) for that same boost level.

metadata.units: Injector pulse width scaling (1 count ~ 1 microsecond / 0.001 ms, range 0 to 65.5 ms)

PTPWOF.raw_text: OVERVIEW: PTPWOF is the boost-onset fuel rate adder for part-throttle driving. Think of it as a progressive power-valve spring and jet combo built into the computer's fuel injection logic. When you are cruising at light throttle, your engine runs on normal manifold vacuum, and the ECU delivers fuel strictly according to your base cruise fuel map (MAPTBL_FuelPartThrottle). But on a turbocharged engine, if you roll into the gas pedal to pass a car or pull up a grade on the highway, the turbo spools up and boosts the intake manifold-even though your foot has not mashed the gas pedal to the floor. As manifold pressure climbs past roughly 5 pounds of boost, air density shoots up rapidly. If the computer only looked at the vacuum cruise fuel map, the mixture would instantly go lean and cause dangerous detonation (spark knock) or a flat-spot stumble. PTPWOF solves this by calculating how far your boost pressure is above that ~5 psi threshold and immediately multiplying that extra pressure by this calibration setting. It adds that extra squirt of fuel directly on top of your normal cruise pulse width, keeping air/fuel ratios safely rich while the turbo builds boost, all without washing down the cylinders during normal light-load vacuum cruise. | TUNER'S GUIDE: Physical Effects of Raising vs. Lowering: Raising the Value (Richer Boost Spool): Delivers more extra fuel for every pound of boost you make under part-throttle acceleration. If your engine feels like it hesitates, surges, or pings as boost begins building at half-throttle, bumping this value up will richen the mixture and smooth out turbo spool-up. Lowering the Value (Leaner Boost Spool): Decreases the extra fuel added per pound of boost. If the car stumbles, puffs black smoke, or feels sluggish and boggy when rolling into boost at partial throttle, lowering this value will clean up the transition. Edge Cases: Setting to Zero: Completely disables the part-throttle boost adder. The engine will receive zero supplemental fuel as boost builds until either wide-open throttle is hit or the computer maxes out the base cruise table. This will cause a severe lean condition, backfiring through the intake, or piston-damaging detonation under part-throttle boost! Setting to Maximum: Forces the boost-added pulse width to jump straight to the full-throttle ceiling (WOTTBL) the moment you cross the boost threshold (~5 psi). While fuel delivery will not exceed what the engine gets at wide-open throttle due to the safety clamp, having full WOT fueling at mere partial throttle will make the engine run excessively rich, causing sluggish spool-up, soggy acceleration, and black exhaust smoke. Real-World Tuning Scenarios: Why Upgrading to a 3-Bar MAP Sensor Requires RAISING This Setting: A 2-bar MAP sensor reads from full vacuum up to ~14.7 psi of boost across its full voltage range. A 3-bar sensor squeezes double the boost range (up to ~29.4 psi) across that same voltage range. Because each unit of voltage on a 3-bar sensor represents 50% more pressure, the computer sees fewer counts per pound of boost (it counts 1.5 times slower). If you left this setting alone after swapping to a 3-bar sensor, the computer would only add about 67% of the extra fuel it used to add for every pound of boost, causing the engine to lean out during part-throttle spool-up! Rule of thumb for 3-bar conversion: Multiply this setting by 1.5 (a 50% increase) to restore the factory fuel adder rate per pound of boost. (You will also lower OBCONST from 170 down to 113 to keep the boost trigger at ~5 psi). Why Upgrading to Larger Injectors (+20%, +40%, etc.) Requires LOWERING This Setting: Larger injectors flow more fuel for every millisecond the nozzle is pulsed open. If you install +40% injectors (which flow ~1.4 times as much fuel), leaving this pulse width adder alone will squirt 40% too much fuel into the engine, causing it to bog and puff black smoke when the turbo spools at partial throttle. Rule of thumb for injector changes: Divide this setting by your injector flow multiplier (e.g., divide by 1.20 for +20% injectors, or divide by 1.40 for +40% injectors). The Combined Real-World Math (3-Bar MAP + Bigger Injectors): Notice that upgrading to a 3-bar MAP pulls this setting UP (x 1.5), while bigger injectors pull this setting DOWN (/ 1.4). When you do both at the same time, the two changes partially cancel each other out: New Setting = Base Setting * 1.5 (for 3-bar) / Injector Multiplier For example, moving from a stock 2-bar setup with stock injectors (stock setting ~7,858) to a 3-bar setup with +20% to +40% injectors results in a net setting of ~9,451 (an overall increase of ~20%), exactly as configured in Stage IV calibrations! Bigger Turbochargers & Aggressive Cams: Large aftermarket turbos often build boost later and hit harder. If your wideband O2 gauge shows a brief lean spike right as the turbo hits 5-10 psi under medium pedal travel, nudge this value up 5% to 10% to provide the necessary fuel cushion to keep combustion stable and exhaust gas temperatures safe.
